govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NitrateTest_Nit:
General Atomic of San Diego wrote this letter on August 12, 1968, to Howard L. Roffman. The company notes that its work on the Oswald case is reported in General Atomic Report GA-6152. Appended to the letter are neutron-activation analysis results, run on hand blanks from shooting cases.

Neutron-activation analysis was the era's high-technology test for bullet lead and gunshot residue. Laboratories measured trace elements to link samples, or to rule links out. The hand blanks were control samples, the baseline against which a shooter's hands were compared. The letter and its tables show a defense contractor's laboratory doing forensic work for the Oswald debate, and reporting it in the flat form of test results.

During Jimmy Carter's presidency, United States officials drew up a highly sensitive blacklist of Colombian officials they believed were corrupt. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, posted in April 2024, which brought that list to light. The names had stayed secret for decades.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Saturday, October 27, 1962 was the most dangerous single day of the Cuban Missile Crisis. This briefing book was posted exactly sixty years later, on October 27, 2022. It gathers declassified records on those twenty-four hours.

By that Saturday the standoff over Soviet missiles in Cuba had reached its peak strain. American forces were on high alert and both leaders faced choices that could start a nuclear war. A day-by-day documentary record lets readers slow the crisis down and see how close the decisions came, hour by hour, to disaster. It remains the standard example of a crisis survived by hours.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
On September 9, 1949, Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter handed President Harry Truman a carefully worded report. It described abnormal radioactive contamination in the Northern Pacific, far above normal atmospheric levels. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted seventy years later in September 2019.

The contamination was the fingerprint of the first Soviet nuclear test, which had ended the American atomic monopoly years earlier than expected. Detection by air sampling, not by spies, was the breakthrough. The documents trace how scientists confirmed the finding and how it was phrased for a president. Every later nuclear monitoring system descends from this first success.

In early August 1977, Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev wrote directly to President Jimmy Carter with an alarming report. Soviet surveillance had detected a nuclear weapons test site in South Africa. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2023, on that discovery and what followed.

Brezhnev asked the United States to act on the finding. A Soviet warning to Washington about an ally of the West is one of the Cold War's stranger cooperative moments. Joint pressure did follow, and South Africa's test was called off. The documents show rivals sharing intelligence when a new bomb program threatened them both.

John Finnemore wrote many such tales for boys. His schools run on fairness enforced by heroes. This opening is the genre in miniature. Readers of Tom Brown will know the country.
19967-beauty-and-the-beast:
Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, retold here anonymously. The merchant's family has fallen into poverty. With no servants, the girls must work hard, like peasants. The sons cultivate the fields to earn their living. All live roughly clothed and simply. That fall from wealth sets Beauty's story in motion. A stolen rose will carry her to the Beast's castle.

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont's version shaped this tale for children. Her Beauty is virtuous, dutiful, and brave in that order. The Beast's courtesy slowly disproves his appearance. Generations learned the tale in forms close to this one. Its lesson, that worth hides under roughness, never dates. This retelling keeps the familiar bones clean.
20018-evenings-at-donaldson-manor-or-the:
Maria J. McIntosh wrote Evenings at Donaldson Manor, also called The Christmas Guest. Its frame gathers guests for Christmas evenings of talk and tales. A quoted review praises McIntosh's Woman in America warmly here. She has written a clever book, the Protestant Churchman says. It contains much good word and truth, the review continues. American ladies are urged to consider her thoughts carefully. The manor evenings continue that improving vein.

McIntosh was a popular Southern writer of moral fiction. Her Christmas frame lets stories teach without sermonizing directly. Donaldson Manor's guests debate conduct, faith, and feeling nightly. The format suits holiday reading by the fire. American ladies were her declared audience and market. The book shows domestic fiction's respectable power.
20022-sequil-or-things-whitch-aint-finis:
Henry A. Shute wrote Sequil in 1904 as the sequel to his Plupy books. Its narrator Plupy keeps a diary in cheerfully bad spelling. He has forgot whether it was brite and fair since his last diry, he writes. Anyway, it is brite and fair today; lots of things have happened. Beany's father is a policeman now, which makes Beany feel pretty big. Plupy warns Beany had better not say much to him anyway.

Shute, a New Hampshire judge, wrote the Real Diary of a Real Boy first. Its misspelled boyhood became a national delight. Sequil continues Plupy's schoolboy wars, pranks, and loyalties. The comedy lives in the spelling and the deadpan alike. Grown readers remembered their own diaries in his. These books are American boyhood classics of their decade.
21133-true-to-his-colours-the-life-that-:
Crossbourne, a quiet village among hills, is the scene of the Reverend Theodore P. Wilson's tale of a sceptic's home. Wilson sets his story some forty years before he wrote, in a place that seemed to hide from the roaring traffic around it. A stream runs restlessly through the village day and night.

True to His Colours argues, in story form, for the life that wears best: steady Christian faith over drink and doubt. Long sermons run through the narrative, as Wilson's readers expected from his temperance fiction. The village cast works out questions of belief, drink, and duty in their daily rounds and troubles.
21298-the-black-tor-a-tale-of-the-reign-:
Two teenage boys from feuding families meet among the wild hills of Derbyshire's Peak District. George Manville Fenn sets their tale in the reign of James the First, their families locked in a centuries-old feud. Each lives in a castle above the moors. A band of ex-soldiers camps on the hills and descends to rob the poorer folk.

The boys form a secret alliance, gathering their fathers' workmen into a small private army against the raiders. Their first attack fails badly. With better weapons and a better plan they try again. Fenn sets honour, inherited hate, and common danger against each other, letting the feud's youngest heirs end what their fathers could not.
21311-gil-the-gunner-the-youngest-office:
Gilbert Vincent goes out to India as a very young soldier in George Manville Fenn's long tale of the East. Schoolboy fights open the book before the regiment sails. In India, battles follow in quick order, and Gil is wounded, knocked out, and recovering as often as he fights.

At one point a wealthy local rajah captures Gil and treats him like an honoured guest, offering him any jewels he likes. Gil refuses, saying freedom to return to his father in the regiment is worth more than gems. The fighting aims at pushing the British out of India, and Fenn follows its cost on both sides.
21313-in-honour-s-cause-a-tale-of-the-da:
Frank Gowan, seventeen, is a page in the Prince of Wales's anteroom at the court of George the First. His father serves in the King's Guard, while fellow page Andrew leans Jacobite, like his father. George Manville Fenn fills the Hanoverian court with German and Dutch courtiers the king brought for comfort.

A German baron deliberately insults Frank's father, and their duel leaves the baron badly wounded. Though loyal to the king, Sir Robert Gowan is sentenced to lose his regiment and leave the country. Frank's search for his father runs through rooftop escapes, spies, and disguises around St James's Palace and its park.
21378-yussuf-the-guide-or-the-mountain-b:
Lawrence, a consumptive boy in his late teens with no relations, wishes aloud for a holiday somewhere hot and sunny. His doctor and a retired professor agree to take him to Asia Minor to see the antiquities, under his lawyer guardian's eye. George Manville Fenn sends the party first to Greece.

Dishonest ship crews sour the start, though their luggage went safely ahead. In Turkey they hire Yussuf, a charming and resourceful guide, and travel inland as helpfulness thins town by town. Mountain bandits capture the party at last and demand a ransom. Yussuf's skill becomes their best hope, in Fenn's tale of sickness, travel, and escape.
21384-afar-in-the-forest:
A young settler tells the tale in W. H. G. Kingston's Afar in the Forest, a short novel of life in the wild woods. He hunts game for the family store while his Uncle Mark fells tall trees around their home. Bit by bit, the two clear land at their new place.

Much of the book is Uncle Mark's own story, told by the fire at night. He tells why the family left home, how they landed safe, and how they found an old settlement in ruins. Lost kin, hidden ties, and two rescued children give the tale its twists. Kingston keeps the cast tangled on purpose, so close reading pays off.
21464-the-gilpins-and-their-fortunes-a-s:
Two school leavers talk over their futures at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Gilpins. One Gilpin boy dreams, with his brother, of farming in Australia like their hard-working father. The brothers sail, and their luck turns on a Sydney quay.

There they save a family from a carriage with bolting horses, and win strong friends. The friends place them as overseers of a run-down sheep and cattle station past the Blue Mountains. The old manager was a crook, and many hands, sent out for crimes, are idle or worse. Mutiny brews before the brothers can set things right.
21493-twice-lost:
Godfrey Rayner's father, a half-pay naval lieutenant, joins a Bristol merchant house in W. H. G. Kingston's Twice Lost. The boy ships as a midshipman on the Heroine for the Pacific. There the tale's lost boy, Harry, first comes into view.

Islanders hold a shipwrecked sailor, and Harry proves to be an English boy used as a pearl diver. The crew takes him aboard and frees him from cruel masters. Years later the party settles in Australia, on the station next to Harry's own parents. Chance and grit drive this warm, tidy tale of loss and return.
21495-to-the-west:
Two young clerks quit a tyrant of an auctioneer in George Manville Fenn's To the West. They set their sights on British Columbia, far across the sea. The way there runs round Cape Horn to San Francisco, then up the coast.

On the road they meet folk good and bad, as Fenn's heroes always do. At last they reach the north and turn to hunting gold. Fenn draws places he never saw with striking life and care. The book runs long for him, some fifteen hours read aloud, and keeps its pace through storms, claims, and close calls.
21558-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
King Charles flees toward the New Forest as Captain Marryat's The Children of the New Forest opens. Marryat published the tale in 1847, his twenty-fourth book and the last of his lifetime. It was written for children and has stayed in print ever since.

When their father falls for the king, the Beverley children hide in a forester's cottage. They learn to farm, hunt, and live by their own hands. Roundhead foes and loyal friends test their courage and wit. The book's blend of history, woodcraft, and family love made it a lasting classic of children's fiction.
21676-confessions-of-a-caricaturist:
Oliver Herford confesses his art in Confessions of a Caricaturist, published in 1917 and dedicated to William Dean Howells. Short verses sit beside drawings of famed men, from Napoleon to Saint Paul. Herford likes Napoleon best, he says, since one hand hides in his vest.

Drawing hands, he owns, is not his knack, and Napoleon spares him the trouble. Roosevelt, Kipling, Shaw, Morgan, and Rockefeller take their turns in rhyme. Even Dante gets a joke about Benedictine and Chianti. Herford's light touch made him the wittiest pen-and-pencil man of his New York circle.
21734-the-golden-dream-adventures-in-the:
Gold in the far West draws the cast of this Ballantyne adventure across an ocean and a continent. The golden dream of the title is the hope of quick wealth that pulled thousands west in his century. Ballantyne knew the wild side of North America from his own years in Canada. He sets green newcomers against a land that tests every promise it seems to make.

The tale follows the party through travel, work, and danger in the western wilds. Greed, luck, and friendship pull the story in turn. Ballantyne keeps his moral steady: wealth found too fast can cost more than it pays. Young readers of his day took the warning with the adventure, gladly.
21753-the-norsemen-in-the-west:
Greenland eight or nine hundred years ago opens this Ballantyne tale of the Norsemen who reached America before Columbus. Two shaggy figures in bear-like dress creep over a ridge above a small hamlet of cottages, sheds, sheep, and boats. A sturdy settler plays with his small son outside the main cottage. The scene sets a whole lost world in motion.

Ballantyne follows the Norse settlers west from Greenland toward the new lands beyond the sea. Voyages, meetings with native peoples, and the hardships of a far colony fill the tale. He wrote it to give boys a true old story: that Europeans crossed the Atlantic long before Columbus. History and adventure sail in the same boat here.
21823-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Tiny field creatures gather for a feast in this small book of verse by R. M. Ballantyne, published in 1874 for very young children. The gadfly blows his trumpet to call the company: beetle, emmet, gnat, and dragonfly all come in their colors. Predators lay aside their wars for the day and join the dance. A few over-eager dancers cause small mishaps, all safely mended.

Ballantyne wrote half a dozen such books for the youngest readers, some under the name Comus. This one is perhaps a twentieth the size of his sea novels. The rhymes are simple, merry, and meant to be read aloud. It shows the great adventure writer playing gently at the nursery door.
21871-adventures-in-the-far-west:
Young Britons cross the North American West in this short, picture-filled adventure by W. H. G. Kingston. Twenty-nine illustrations crowd the book, including a striking scene of a witch doctor visiting a sick man. The party travels among grizzly bears, wolves, and tribes who do not want them there. For much of the tale they live with a friendly tribe, whose ways Kingston describes at length.

Near the end, the heroes help rescue an emigrant wagon train attacked by a hostile tribe. A young lady has been seized and carried off, and the chase is on. Charley Fielding's cry at the campfire opens the action. Kingston's style, the editor says, is as excellent as ever. It is a brisk western in his classic mold.
22042-christmas-its-origin-and-associati:
William Francis Dawson set out to trace Christmas from its beginnings to his own day. His Christmas: Its Origin and Associations gathers customs scattered through many older authors. He found that some great Christmas feasts marked turning points in English history. He also saw the yearly feast as a link in the chain of Christian evidence across nineteen centuries.

Dawson moves from Roman and pagan roots through medieval revels to Victorian family practice. Holly, mistletoe, carols, feasts, and charity all get their histories. The book is earnest, well stocked, and proud of its subject. It suits readers who want the story behind the holiday's familiar trimmings.
22277-darry-the-life-saver-or-the-heroes:
Frank V. Webster wrote Darry the Life Saver, or The Heroes of the Coast, in 1911 for boy readers. Webster supplied many volumes to the cheap series trade under his own name and others. His hero Darry belongs to the surfmen who guarded America's coasts. The book opens on a brigantine battered by a Caribbean hurricane, staggering along like a wounded beast, her masts gone by the board.

From that wreck the tale builds rescues by breeches buoy and lifeboat. One picture shows a woman lowered safely and stowed away. The Life-Saving Service, forerunner of the Coast Guard, supplies real practice behind the thrills. Darry's adventures honour men who rowed out when others ran from the sea.
